summary:
Angola's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and, in the same instrument, made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment. A continental survey published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression are located across Title II of the same document.

No specific Angolan law authorises a transgender person to change the gender marker on identity documents or passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states in general that details entered into registration records should not be altered, but section 87 gives the Civil Registrar broad authority to make changes, including changes of name and changes where a shift in facts alters a person's legal identity and status. The practical effect is that a marker change may be possible through that discretionary route rather than through an established procedure, and the sources do not document how registrars have used it. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49 per cent of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola. Social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant, and an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony held in 2005 was reported in national news magazines as 'shameless' and 'abominable'.

Dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are absent from the record: no shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or comparable dedicated services are recorded anywhere in the sources. People living with HIV/AIDS are entitled by law to health care services and to protection from discrimination in employment.

No entry or visa provisions specific to Angola are recorded in the inventory. The only entry-adjacent material consists of external reference links: an asylum-law information packet on sexual minorities and HIV status, and travel advice on local laws and customs from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

Recent documentation points to continuing harm despite decriminalisation. A shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter, submitted for the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024 by Angolan organisations including Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA and Diversidade Masculina with international support, documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. A separate submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, ahead of the committee's 74th session review of Angola, raises discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.

Organised support exists but is narrow. Two LGBT groups operate in Angola, and only one, the Iris Angola Association, has official legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018; at that time it had around 200 members, based in the capital with offices in Benguela and Lubango.
tangentialFactors:
Trans visibility in Angola has preceded legal protection rather than followed it. In April 2012 the BBC profiled the kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, who became a mainstream star at 25, in an article describing a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour. The episode indicates that openly gender-nonconforming public figures could achieve wide recognition under the formal criminalisation regime that was only removed in 2021.

Political parties have not made LGBT questions a programme issue: the three major parties have not formally addressed LGBT topics in their platforms. The government does permit non-governmental organisations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education, so organised activity operates through the general NGO framework rather than through a dedicated equality body.

In 2010 the Angolan government refused to receive the openly gay incoming Israeli ambassador, Isi Yanouka, at a diplomatic reception, a decision attributed to his sexual orientation. The source characterises this as a reception decision rather than a visa rule, and it does not establish a formal entry bar.

Angola's 2019 statute is repeatedly measured against legislative drafting elsewhere on the continent, where states have chosen different routes: retaining or repealing colonial offences, and whether or not to attach penalties to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.
localsOnly:
Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded. The first association, Acção Humana, launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programmes specifically for LGBT people have struggled to attract NGO money. An HIV/AIDS educational programme for LGBT people is only beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International.

A 2007 study estimated that roughly five per cent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men. Residents living with HIV/AIDS hold an entitlement to health care services and to protection against discrimination in employment, while the practical availability of that care and the enforcement of that protection are not documented in the inventory.

Residents face the absence of shelters, safe houses and gender-neutral facilities, and the social expectation of opposite-sex marriage. The three major political parties have not adopted LGBT positions, and the state's formal equality machinery rests on the 2019 statute's prohibition of sexual-orientation discrimination rather than on a constitutional guarantee listing gender or sexual orientation among protected grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
No entry or visa provisions for Angola are sourced in this inventory. The only entry-adjacent material is external: an asylum-law information packet covering sexual minorities and HIV status, and UK government travel advice on local laws and customs. Any specific visa, arrival screening or border-question practice remains unresolved on the present record.

The inventory contains no youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education for Angola, and none should be inferred.

Whether the Civil Registrar has in practice used section 87 of the 2015 Código do Registo Civil to authorise gender-marker changes, and what documentation or court involvement that route requires, is unresolved: the source identifies the discretionary authority but supplies no cases, statistics or procedure.

Enforcement of the 2019 prohibition on sexual-orientation discrimination is not documented. The inventory records the penalty attaching to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services, and separately records recent shadow-report and treaty-body documentation of continuing violations against LGBTQI+ people, but supplies no enforcement figures, prosecutions or complaints outcomes linking the two.
